Using the distinctive features of the Standard Model, particularly the $t\bar{t}$ production from elastic scattering, we propose a method to detect top quarks through inelastic scattering. By applying an optimized selection process and analysis, we aim to identify top-quark events in data from the LHC with the CMS detector, specifically from $\sqrt{s}=8$ TeV proton-proton collisions, with 2 files containing 19.9 inverse femtobarns of data. To find the top quark signal, we leverage variables that precisely measure the top quark pair's transverse momentum and utilize simulated top-quark production from both LO and NLO levels of QCD. If certain conditions are met regarding the accuracy of the top quark mass and the transverse momentum of protons, this method can potentially reveal top quark production at the LHC, or otherwise establish lower bounds on these properties to further investigate with higher luminosity or increased energy.

A graph G is considered strongly Ramsey-rich if, for any two colorings of the graph that are not interchangeable through a symmetry of the graph, there are at least three distinct elements that are colored differently in the two colorings' edges. When an infinite graph is divided into connected parts, we say it is infinitely strongly Ramsey-rich if each of these parts is strongly Ramsey-rich. Similar definitions of being strongly or infinitely strongly Ramsey-rich apply to hypergraphs. 

In the case of two-colored complete spacefills, whose sections are also known as bipartite subgraphs, we establish that being infinitely strongly Ramsey-rich is the highest level of property. Moreover, any infinite graph that is not infinitely strongly or just strongly Ramsey-rich, when combined with all possible edges, will always result in at least four distinct outcomes that are colored differently in two different symmetry-related graph arrangements. A key feature of this study is that being infinitely strongly Ramsey-rich, being strongly Ramsey-rich, and having an infinite number of edges not part of any closed loops, are all equivalent characteristics of bipartite structures. A crucial finding from Erdos, Hahn, and Mount (1976) is also given a new, distinct proof.

Our qutrit-based implementation of scalar QED in its simplest dimensionless form exhibits a few intriguing characteristics.  Despite being an $O(c)$ algorithmic method, it displays sublinear scaling in both lattice size and time.  It also achieves a fivefold pressure maintenance capability across five times the system size and five times the number of Monte Carlo iterations. In addition, it performs a five-times more frequent quantum evolution per second.

Quantum electrodynamics predictions suggest that high-energy particle collisions can produce a dense pool of polarized positrons. These sources are vital for several types of experiments involving intense light. While traditional methods for creating these sources rely on high-energy particles, new techniques using ultra-powerful lasers interacting with thin metal films show great potential. Our research reveals that such lasers can create a dense pool of polarized positrons with high energy and spin alignment. Specifically, the positron cloud is predicted to have high density, high polarization levels, and high energy. These sources are anticipated to be valuable for various experiments, including those involving weak nuclear forces, time-reversal symmetry, and scalar particles.

This paper explores the concept of algebraic diameter of finite groups when generated by two elements, den as $d(G,s_1,s_2)$, and seeks to identify conditions under which this value is finite for a given group. Building on the findings of our recent preprint, we establish that if a group contains a subgroup with a finite diameter and is a solvable extension of it, then the group has a finite diameter. Furthermore, we provide evidence for a conjecture stating that all groups with sub-exponential diameter contain groups with polynomial diameter as their leading term, including results on specific families of groups and a probabilistic proof of the same for most groups with a polynomial diameter.

To better adapt embedded systems to temperature-sensitive applications, it is crucial to incorporate designs that can automatically adjust settings based on temperature changes. To achieve this, we developed a novel small size temperature detector with key features including a broad operating voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, a very low power consumption at ambient temperatures, an extremely low temperature sensitivity of 0.24°C, a relatively large temperature detection range of 2.8V, and an innovative direct temperature sensing method. An experimental results on an 11-stage 0.18μm CMOS process revealed a very small chip size of 0.004 square millimeters, a complete temperature sensitivity of 1.06nJ per conversion, and correct performance within the specified voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V.
In this study, the conventional differential geometric concepts typically associated with manifolds are re-expressed using Lie groupoids and smooth stacks as underlying frameworks.

Recent high-sensitivity observations in the mid-infrared spectrum around the 4.5 micrometer hydrogen emission feature of Dragon IRD (IRAS 22223-7541), famously known as the "Dragon", have been used to remove the background noise. Removing this artifact reveals a distinctly dense central core surrounded by the emission on either side. This core's density profile follows a power law with a steep slope, indicative of gravitational collapse or a significant, localized densification process. We hypothesize that this phenomenon could be the initial stage in the formation of massive stars, with no evidence yet present to suggest it's a region being cleared out by a massive outflow. Analysis also shows that the Dragon has undergone a transformation from a typical molecular outflow region to an emerging class of embedded protostars.

Recurrence relations are essential in the context of imaging and image processing issues, as they accelerate computational efficiency and simplify boundary condition imposition. Basically, these relations link Bessel functions with powers of their arguments, allowing for their derivation from differential equations. However, for any scenario where the Bessel functions represent the elements of a stationary random field, an appropriate recurrence relation links adjacent functions with local spatial interactions. We introduce and examine two methods for obtaining such recurrence relations for a general linear stochastic field defined on the sphere. The first method defines a probability distribution over the sphere, leading to an asymptotically flat recurrence relation, while the second relates the spectral components in the plane wave expansion, resulting in an exact, sphere-independent recurrence relation. These relationships are applied to the Gaussian random field, producing an expression for the correlation function in real space, and can also be utilized in modeling other linear random fields.

The friction coefficient of dry foam packs dry granular materials and bubble clusters, consisting of solid bubble plates, in ways that are analogous to each other. The friction within foam packs is primarily influenced by the size of the bubble plates, rather than their shape, in line with findings from previous studies on granular media. The absence of a correlation between friction and the aspect ratio of the plate jammed pack's friction was noted, the average aspect ratio of 1 being too close in value to each other to allow for a meaningful comparison. The model predicts the friction coefficient will increase as the the area of the plate per unit area increases, the integer part of 1 being too close in value to each other to allow for a meaningful difference.

This report details the findings of our research, which aims to develop a effective method for classifying skin lesions into benign and malignant categories using a combination of image processing, deep learning, and entropy analysis. A balanced dataset was used in our study, consisting of 7,398 clinical photos of skin lesions from patients in Italy. We employed a ResNet-50 neural network to extract deep features from the lesion images and utilized Support Vector Machines (SVM) to classify them. Our results demonstrate that this approach achieves an overall accuracy of 97.7% in identifying skin lesions, with a sensitivity of 98.4% and a specificity of 97.0%. Additionally, we used the dermoscopy images to detect outlier samples and discovered that 2.44% of the data set contained atypical lesions, with 4,356 images classified as benign and 88 as malignant.

A spinning Hele-Shaw cell featuring a viscous fluid and an air interface shows unstable fingers that extend into the container's center due to centrifugal force. The research rates the finger instability's growth rate using two methods: linear theory and phase-field modeling. The study reveals that centrifugal force causes the surface tension to behave differently, leading to a unique pattern of finger width variation. The results also show that increased rotation speeds lead to narrower fingers, in addition to changes in rotation speed impacting the shape of the finger profiles. The findings provide valuable insights into results observed in rotating tanks.

A striking discovery of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5C2H) has been made in the TMC-1 molecular cloud, prompting a re-evaluation of saturation-derived hydrocarbon ring species. Alongside this, the evidence for ethynyl furan (THF) previously attributed to a spectroscopic assignment error has been debunked. A notable discrepancy between the observed abundance of cyano derivatives and the predicted ethynyl levels within the molecule has also been highlighted, with a similar pattern previously observed in the Thiolase molecule but explicably resolved. These discoveries underscore the limited understanding of highly unsaturated hydrocarbon ring species, with a strong case made for the essential role they may have in interstellar chemistry, with a particular focus on carbon-rich environments.

In many aspects of human language processing, speakers listen to future input with ease, and this capability is difficult to replicate using automatic translation systems. A more technical issue arises when translating languages that place the object before the verb, as established by Universal Grammar. Neural networks typically rearrange objects correctly, but they struggle to place verbs in the expected subject - verb order. In our investigation, we find that even when trained with losses that account for function words, models fail to position verbs accurately. We believe listening can be emulated more effectively through the use of attention mechanisms that look ahead, and we propose a novel architecture, Look-Ahead Neural Attention (LANA), for translation that incorporates these mechanisms. Experimentally, LANA demonstrates a simple yet effective method for generating correct function word and attachment patterns, as well as improving overall translation quality.

The framework approach to software engineering is widely used for developing complex software projects, providing structure and clarity. A key aspect of frameworks is distinguishing between abstract components that make up the system's architecture and a supporting infrastructure that facilitates the system's operation without directly contributing to its functionality. This paper examines a case study involving the Translational Grid Framework (TGF), an open-source tool that enables the creation of grid applications by leveraging existing infrastructure. We argue that tools like TGF are better described as based on a translational framework rather than a traditional framework, and introduce a new component to supporting infrastructure called "supporting interfaces." These interfaces, a key innovation of TGF, are specialized tools that bridge the gap between the components of a grid application and those of the supporting infrastructure, including the underlying infrastructure itself. Consequently, we propose that tools such as TGF and their underlying translational frameworks are best characterized as consisting of three parts: components that make up the system's architecture, a translational engine, and a set of tools for creating tools like a programming language, a development environment, and other essential tools.

A new theoretical framework, called the combined dark fluid model with combined dark component $\theta$ and dissipative dissipation component $\pi$, is proposed. This model is governed by a single fluid, but with two distinct parts that satisfy different fluid equations. The model is entirely classical and lacks the spinor field, seen in analogous nonholonomic geometries. A rigorous mathematical analysis reveals that a unique solution, where the two components become indistinguishable, results in an effective F(R) gravity. A star, applied to this gravity model, is calculated and compared to the observed neutron star, demonstrating that this dark fluid representation is applicable even to highly dense stellar objects.

Both neutrino and dark sector theories based on effective field theories propose new interactions that could lead to $J/\psi$ decays into visible photons and invisible neutrinos or scalars via the Stark effect. A study aims to establish rigorous constraints on these hypothetical scenarios by comparing their predictions with observed $J/\psi$ decay patterns, particularly the measured single-photon decay rate and lower limit on two-photon decay rates. This research results in more stringent constraints than previously obtained, specifically defining the coupling constants for neutrino and dark sector theories and limiting the possible new particles responsible for $J/\psi$ decays into one visible and one invisible particle.

This research focuses on advancing Multivariate Functional Singular Spectrum Analysis (MFSSA) by refining the traditional approach and offering a robust alternative using weighted Gram - Matthews distances. While MFSSA has been effective in recent years, it's limited to univariate functions. In contrast, this study's modification enables cross-variable analysis and incorporates a distance-based method to manage data outliers. The effectiveness of both techniques is verified through artificial datasets, and their practical application is demonstrated through the examination of oxygen saturation (SpO2) pulse volume pulse waves using both the modified approach and the weighted distances method.

A random walk on the integer line is considered to have a balance between mass and duration if one condition is met: the walk covers all integers within a certain distance without visiting the same point too frequently. Another study also marks a balance for walks that spend a long time within a limited range of integers. This paper is concerned with a few properties related to balance, specifically whether these properties hold forever, how long they last, and how often they occur. It is found that walks can count on infinite balance, but their duration may not last as long, with an average duration that is finite and one that follows a power law with an index of $-2$. Moreover, there is an asymptotic chance of any walk lasting as long as another, and they also share the same average duration.

The IShTAR plasma facility is designed to investigate the helicon mode of high-frequency plasmas, as this mode is suitable for semiconductor processing and stellarator fueling. The device has three distinct operational modes, including the helicon mode, and is powered by plasma generators that are DC, RF, and ICRF matched to the helicon mode for optimal performance. In order to utilize all available power sources effectively, the helicon mode must be matched with RF and ICRF powers using mode converters. The IShTAR plasma generator has been operated in the helicon mode, and the resulting plasmas are characterized in terms of density, temperature, and confinement time. The highest plasma densities are measured at $10^{12}$ cm$^{-3}$, and the temperatures are between 2-5 eV when powered with 100W of RF power. When combined with 2kW of ICRH power, the densities are between 3-6 x $10^{11}$ cm$^{-3}$ with temperatures between 1-2 eV. These measurements are taken with an electron cyclotron frequency of 3.7 GHz, 4 inches of toroidal distance, and 2000 seconds of linear distance, and are obtained when magnetically confined in toroidal geometry.

The microscopic examination of tissue samples for cancer diagnosis involves the detailed analysis of cellular components, where the nucleus serves as a key distinguishing feature between healthy and malignant tissue. Due to the subtle size and color differences between nuclei, even slightly, their accurate detection in microscopic images remains a challenging task. In this study, we introduce a novel two-part convolutional network architecture tailored for the precise identification of nuclei in histopathology images. Our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results on public datasets, specifically with a mean detection score of 0.75, surpassing the best existing results from prior research.

We demonstrate the local converse theorem for all odd-dimensional special orthogonal and symplectic matrices of particular types for all scenarios and all prime numbers. This means the collection of local Gamma factors from the Greenberg-Oshike constants determines all odd-dimensional special orthogonal and symplectic matrices of particular types in all cases and all fields of finite characteristic.

Deep Neural Network variations, including the Graph Convolutional Neural Network, have been widely studied recently. Specifically, the GCNN's operation has been modelled through matching statistics for linked nodes in a graph, enabling it to accurately represent certain real-world applications. However, our investigation reveals that GCNN's fundamental principles go beyond this, as we demonstrate that a simpler operation called matched filtering, closely tied to the adjacency matrix, perfectly mirrors the GCNN's behavior. Unlike the matching filter, the matched filtering method involves using both incoming and outgoing connections from a node, which aligns with the GCNN's iteration that connects nodes in a more intricate manner. Through notable applications and comprehensive numerical experiments, the equivalence between GCNN's complex iterations and the matched filtering operation's simplicity become evident and distinguishable.

We expand the concept of hair in rotating black holes and solitons by incorporating gravity, a scalar field, and a Chern-Simons gauge field. This expansion enables us to re-express the outcomes of numerous studies on "hairy" black holes and solitons in terms of an effective two-dimensional gravity that includes a coupling to a U(1) Chern-Simons gauge field at the boundary. Leveraging this framework, we successfully described the same rotating hairy black holes and solitons in both dimensions. Moreover, a concise expression for the black holes' mass, demonstrated in this study, reveals its direct proportionality to the square of both the scalar and gauge field charges.

Traditional ultrasound elastography techniques rely on estimating the velocity field from time-resolved data, a process complicated by the ambiguity of the velocity aliasing phenomenon. In search of a solution to accurately recover velocity fields with minimal computational overhead, this study investigates a novel approach, the Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VO-SA) method, to directly reconstruct strain images. By applying the VO-SA approach, we are able to obtain precise velocity and strain estimates, even in areas where conventional methods fail. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the VO-SA approach can be implemented efficiently through an iterative algorithm, yielding real-time results. We validate our approach through both simulations and experimental tests, demonstrating that the VO-SA method outperforms the standard beam-steering approach in terms of accuracy, with minimal computational costs.

Effective and safe AI assistance for human users requires that the AI understands what is intended, particularly in crucial situations. For this to happen, it's important to train supervised models on something akin "intended examples," which ideally should reflect what a perfect, faultless system would produce. We suggest using the algorithms of the same application as these reference examples - an concept we call Rational Pseudocode. The underlying theory posits that since algorithms are fundamental building blocks of software, they should be the basis for teaching models the same subject, something we believe current practices fall short of. We an example we've applied to our $1,000's scale dataset for the CommonSense Reasoning (CSRD) problem with a simple procedure generator, improving results from a baseline by 16%.

Mean-based methods are widely used in diverse applications including those involving large-scale data streams. In this work, we introduce two novel dynamic multi-class groupings algorithms based on the highest dimension. A fully adaptive update rule is established for a changing environment in our $k$-means dynamic grouping framework. Additionally, we develop two specific applications: the DMSDK algorithm achieves a combination bound when integrating square errors, and the DSCD algorithm effectively manages concept drift in settings with limited labeled examples. Both algorithms demonstrate their effectiveness through successful experiments.

A novel classification system for stochastic pursuit-evasion competitions is proposed, organizing a set of state-space dynamic games into hierarchical levels. The first level features simple competitions with symmetric players and a designated goal state, while the second level encompasses competitions with asymmetric players or penalties in the second level further divides them into games with second-level asymmetries consisting of: (a) asymmetries appearing after n steps, (b) immediate asymmetries, and (c) local local asymmetries. The proposed classification provides a framework for state-space dynamic games and has applications in fields like multi-agent path finding, robust route planning, and autonomous vehicle navigation, where agents must make safe decisions among their peers with different levels of asymmetry.

A theoretical investigation into efficient VBS-like vector boson estimation methods for multi-vector boson scattering, particularly for high-energy muon collisions, utilizes parton distribution functions and incorporates the Parton Shower, highlighting the vector boson efficiency's energetic limitations at high energies. Our study employs high-multilicity multi-vector boson scattering processes as a case study, utilizing the PVVV generator, which combines the PVVV approximation with the PPPI method for precise cross-section calculations in various multi-vector boson processes like same-sign WWWW, WWWW, WWWW, and WWWW scattering. Our results indicate the PVVV approximation's reliability for these processes and highlight the vector boson efficiency's energy-dependent behavior, demonstrating a gradual decline in efficiency with increasing center-of-mass energy and variability across different processes and incoming particle types. Our study also reveals the dominance of WW pair production in high-energy scenarios and the significant vector boson suppression in the s-channel, emphasizing the importance of considering higher-order corrections in multi-vector boson processes.

When using a unified neural network to learn multiple tasks based on a model, the performance can significantly improve, but simultaneous inference and learning for multiple tasks can lead to interference and potentially degrade performance. In this study, we investigate this instance learning interference phenomenon in the context of model-based multi-task reinforcement learning (ML). We find that this instance learning interference can obscure the modular properties required for a single system to effectively master multiple tasks with diverse subgoals and states. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel modular system that separates the policy and the model into distinct neural networks, allowing each to focus on a single task. Our proposed modular system that assigns a unique model to each task can successfully learn several complex locomotion tasks in a realistic setting using a unified policy and several separated models. We also show that this model-sharing among tasks is crucial for the success of our proposed system.

We delve into the foundational theorems established by G\"odel and Tarski, as well as variations and extensions thereof, including alternative formulations and expansions on original proofs. Furthermore, we present our own take on the proof of the first theorem.

This paper proves a three spheres theorem for functions in Clifford analysis, under specific conditions. If we consider a compact Lie group G and its associated Lie algebra with root system $\Phi$, and define the Dirac operator D within this algebra, we can establish an upper bound for the norm of eigenfunctions $u$ with respect to a probability measure $\omega$ on the torus $\hat{T}$. The inequality, known as the three spheres inequality, states that the norm of $u$ in a sphere of radius $\gamma$ is bounded by the geometric mean of the norms of $u$ in spheres of radii $r$ and $R$. The paper has three main results: an initial three spheres theorem with constants equal to one, an characterization of such functions, and an extension of this theorem to include functions that satisfy a differential equation defined by the Dirac operator, with associated D-estimates.

Reconstructing inverse problems often involves finding solutions that are not uniquely determined, with an infinite number of possible outcomes. Time-series reconstruction is a critical aspect of geophysical inverse problems. We investigate this particular aspect using electrocardography as an example, leveraging cardiac activity colors to visualize solution quality in terms of data fit. To enhance the visual interpretability of solution spaces, we propose using generative adversarial networks to generate probability distributions, enabling the generation of diverse, underdetermined solution sets. Testing this approach for posterior extraction in electrocardographic inverse problems shows a significant improvement over traditional methods, producing diverse and credible probabilistic realizations.

This research paper investigates the conditions for invariant manifolds in a specific class of differential equations that model dynamical systems. It is shown that, in most cases, there are no quadratic surfaces that remain unchanged over time in the fractional order system. The study extends to the general scenario of invariant surfaces and applies its findings to the Chua's circuit example. It is concluded that, in the fractional order Chua's circuit, there are no invariant surfaces.

Analysis of scintillation in 1.25 GHz data from the bright pulsar B1133+16 near the Galactic Center has been done to investigate the local interstellar medium (LISM) around it. Using a sophisticated model based on the GLEEP survey, researchers computed the line-of-sight scintillation and compared the results with observations from the GUPU project. This comparison allowed them to derive the electron density around the pulsar as $n_e = (5.0 \pm 0.4) \times 10^{-3} ({d}_{\perp}/{\rm pc})^{2} \pm 0.4 \times 10^{-3} \times 10^{-3} \rm{cm}^{-3}$, where $d_{\perp}$ is the distance from the pulsar to the center of the Gum Nebula. This indicates that the surrounding LISM has a spherical shape with a 1.6 pc radius and an average electron density of approximately $5 \times 10^{-3} \rm{cm}^{-3}$. Furthermore, they calculated the local dispersion measure as $DM = (5.0 \pm 0.5) \times 10^{-3} \rm{pc cm}^{-3}$.

A deep neural network called WaveNet has achieved high-quality audio synthesis, but it's cumbersome when used for musical tone generation due to its heavy parametric count and slow inference speed. Although an adaptable version of WaveNet was released to address these problems, it still relies on a large number of parameters, making it difficult to tune and optimize. Our proposed network, called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet, is designed to generate loudness variations and pitch changes more efficiently by utilizing two separate n-grams and dilated convolutions. Our network can produce nearly identical results to the quasi-periodic WaveNet, but it uses significantly fewer parameters, allowing it to be trained end-to-end. Our proposed network is also straightforward to implement, allowing for simple experiment planning and execution. Our method was tested on both the LIBRITTS-2 and LJSpeech datasets, where it outperformed the quasi-periodic WaveNet in terms of pitch estimation accuracy and perceptual quality metrics. Our results showed that our proposed network achieves lower pitch estimation errors and better perceptual quality scores.

The concept of a Morita shadow is introduced as a refinement of the notion of a shadow, which is graphically manipulatable from the perspective of category theory. It is demonstrated that two categories share identical Morita shadows if and only if their Morita equivalences hold. Furthermore, a specific condition under which two categories have identical Morita shadows can be established, which is categorically interpretable as their bicategorical compositions being equal.

The difficulties individuals with hearing impairments face in determining the location of sounds are well-documented. However, creating a model to replicate this process has been relatively unexplored. In this project, a neural network was trained to estimate sound sources' positions in two-dimensional space using spectral and temporal audio features. The network's design incorporated an attention mechanism and a mechanism for handling temporal inputs. The attention mechanism's design was tailored to the specific characteristics of auditory inputs, and the network demonstrated the ability to generalize across inputs sampled at different rates. The designed network achieved high accuracy in our tests and outperformed a commonly used baseline model, while also incorporating a biologically plausible mechanism for sound localization.

The success of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in handling graph data has been quite significant. However, applying deep learning methods effectively to specific types of graphs, particularly weighted graphs, presents challenges due to the lack a well-defined averaging method for feature vectors. This issue arises from the need to conform to Euclidean space requirements. To address this, we propose a novel, space-agnostic GNN framework called Lorentzian Neural Networks (LNNs). LNN framework is designed to model relational graphs using a mixture of pooling operations that adhere to specific geometric constraints. We demonstrate the effectiveness of LNN by training a classification task using the CITESeer dataset, yielding superior results compared to traditional GNN classifications.

This research focuses on solving an inverse problem for a structurally engaged acoustic system. It aims to restore unknown parts of the boundary conditions applied to a structurally engaged acoustic system's boundary, knowing the resulting fluid pressures in the surrounding fluid and the known vibrational frequencies of the system. The unknown boundary conditions are recovered using an iterative level set method, validated with a two-dimensional numerical example based on known system parameters and reconstructed geometry.

We investigate an efficient delay discounting problem for a decision maker whose preferences conform to the Tsallis exponential function, subject to budget constraints. In the context of a single decision, we discover that efficient delay discounting follows a modified power law, a variation of the traditional exponential discounting law. This has multiple practical applications, including the notable Koomey linear time hypothesis and the UCN paradox. Additionally, we examine the UCU paradox and a second ucucu effect that arises from efficient delay discounting in the context of two opposite decisions: consumption and savings.

Substantial gravity offers an updated framework for the standard gravitational theories, featuring a metric $g_{\mu\nu}$ and an auxiliary metric $\clq{g}_{\mu\nu}$, with the latter aiding in reformulating the $R+{\cal Q}$ action through harmonic transformations. This approach ensures the auxiliary metric remains non-degenerate. We refer to the representation where both metrics are expressed in harmonic coordinates as the harmonic gauge, with corresponding conditions defined by $\Box_g \varphi_a^i = 0$ and $\Box_{\clq g}\clq \var_a^i = 0$. These conditions can be systematically derived from the field equations originating from the $R+{\cal Q}$ action. However, we observe that this action does not entirely enforce the harmonic gauge; instead, it modifies the standard harmonic gauge conditions to $\Box_g \var_a^i = f_a^i(g, \var) $ and $\Box_{\clq g}\clq \var_a^i = \clq f_a^i(g,\clq \var)$. We also note that choosing the harmonic gauge as a boundary or initial condition, as previously discussed in literature, is not a valid approach. Instead, we recommend the harmonic gauge conditions be derived from theories like those based on the $R+{\cal Q}$ action, which can be further analyzed using the gauge-fixed perturbation theory.

This research reveals that canonical equilibrium conditions in a given Weyl-Wigner representation must adhere to a set of compatibility conditions that ensure the joint measurability of a specific type of quantum and classical observables. Initially, we provide a set of conditions necessary and sufficient for a collection of Weyl-Wigner functions to correspond to a measurable function on phase space for canonical conditions of the form $\hat{A}_i \rho = \lambda_i \rho$. Furthermore, we examine how these conditions apply to two primary applications: first, to the QRD equation in a given external electromagnetic field, and its associated measure compatibility conditions; and second, to the Boltzman equation in a given external field, and its associated measure compatibility conditions.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this temperature regime, several intriguing phenomena emerge. The passage through points of negative temperature during the adiabatic cooling process enables a direct discovery of quantum degeneracy. As a result, a new quantum phase transition emerges, distinct from its classical counterpart. Moreover, negative temperature gives rise to a re-emergence of the Planck's law in the context of quantum statistics. Furthermore, thermodynamic quantities such as entropy and heat capacity become anomalous, exhibiting behaviors opposite to those observed at positive temperatures. As a consequence, new quantum versions of Dulong-Petit's law and Lamb-Chapelier law are formed. Finally, a re-examination of quantum spin chains reveals that their quantum phase diagram is divided into three distinct regions, separated by three unique quantum critical points.

A minimal extension of the Standard Model is considered, which includes a scalar dark matter candidate and standard SU(2) gauge symmetry. By extending the model with a secondary scalar singlet and doublet, we can account for observed phenomena such as neutrino mass, the weakness of dark matter interactions, and the stability of the vacuum. The parameters chosen for these additional particles also ensure that the dark matter density matches observations, that neutrino masses are appropriate, and that the vacuum remains stable. A key implication of this framework is that the dark matter interaction scale exceeds the electroweak force, which could be detected in future experiments at the Large Hadron Collider or direct dark matter detectors. The research establishes the limits for the dark matter interaction strength, the mass of the doublet scalar, and the connection between these parameters and the dark matter mass. Additionally, the study determines the threshold for dark matter pair-production through the interaction, as well as through the exchange of the scalar singlet. The findings can be represented visually through contour plots illustrating the relationship between key parameters. The research also accounts for corrections introduced by scalar dark matter self-interactions.

Blending of certain electron orbitals in transition metal compounds is often impeded by symmetry restrictions, yet a recent study reveals that these orbitals can combine effectively in materials with spiral magnetic patterns, such as smectic magnetoelectric transverse waves. By applying first-principles methods to 4d and 5d transition metal compounds composed of linear chains, researchers discovered that $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitals blend seamlessly, contrary to common assumptions. This result is extensively supported and compared with experimental data, providing a comprehensive analysis of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbital characteristics in these materials.

This research results from a parallel to topological concepts under rational transformation in quantum topology. In quantum topological entities, a natural analogy to Riemann integration is the quantum trace, which has an essential property called the invariance under coordinate change. In quantum knot theory, we define a new operation, the quantum parallelogram move, representing the quantum analogue to the fundamental theorem of calculus. It turns out that the invariance under rational transformation and the quantum parallelogram move are essentially equivalent. Furthermore, there's a broader framework for three-dimensional link diagrams where the quantum parallelogram move can be applied, enabling us to define a new invariant under rational transformation for links in these diagrams. We demonstrate that this new invariant, when applied to the standard representation of links, is equivalent to the Kauffman invariant.

Effective patient diagnosis relies on effective illness detection, where human
developers' participation is often missing in current datasets where patients' illness
information is absent or inaccurate. This study explores various methods to integrate
illness data into medical images and evaluates the effect of different approaches on
chest X-ray based illness detection. Three methods are investigated: manual
annotation, superposition of illness templates, and deep learning-based style
transfer. This study finds that even basic methods for incorporating illness
information, such as copying and pasting pathology features, can significantly
impact detection performance. Notably, directly modifying X-ray images with
pathology indicators led to an average 6.1 point boost in illness detection,
whereas using a style transfer method resulted in an average 3.5 point decrease
when distinguishing between healthy and ill individuals.

ViDaExpert is an application designed for the interactive visualization and thorough analysis of high-dimensional vector content. This tool enables users to engage in a wide range of linear and non-linear examination methods, including scaling, folding, and other operations, while also supporting the visualization history H5 format for preserving and retrieving past sessions, along with HPC-friendly efficiency.
